extracted.intended_audience: readers and writers (early-18th-century London) — especially authors, playwrights, actors, and merchants (Spectator's polite public)
extracted.subtask_description: A series of Spectator essays giving prescriptive advice and evaluative criteria about authorship honesty, theatrical performance, commercial fairness, club election procedure, and the moral aims of poetry and praise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honesty of an author in the sale of his ware
rubrics_metrics.description: An author ought to own all that he had borrowed from others, and lay in a clear light all that he gives his Spectators for their Money, with an Account of the first Manufacturers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steele condemns passing off others' work as one's own; the author should publicly acknowledge translations or borrowings rather than let readers be deceived. This is presented as an ethical obligation akin to commercial honesty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of exceptions when selling goods
rubrics_metrics.description: It is unjust to make any Step towards Gain, wherein the Gain of even those to whom you sell is not also consulted; a Man is no better than a Cheat who sells any thing without telling the Exceptions against it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice for traders: be transparent about defects and limitations of goods. Example: Mr. John Moreton, after misfortune, sets up a ready-money shop and affixes the value of each piece to the piece itself so even an ignorant buyer can be secure. Encourages ready-money trade, fixed per-piece prices, and avoidance of credit that obscures true value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affixing value and simple pricing to protect buyers
rubrics_metrics.description: He imposes upon himself a Rule of affixing the Value of each Piece he sells to the Piece it self; so that the most ignorant Servant or Child will be as good a Buyer at his Shop as the most skilful in the Trade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical merchant guideline: label items with explicit prices and avoid practices that require specialized knowledge to buy fairly. Presented as both morally preferable and economically advantageous to customers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of audience/performer partiality when judging plays
rubrics_metrics.description: At rehearsals the House was so partial to one of their own Fraternity, that they gave every thing which was said such Grace, Emphasis, and Force in their Action, that it was no easy matter to make any Judgment of the Performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers/critics should note that actors and sympathetic audiences can make a performance appear better than it might be in impartial view; judge texts and performances with awareness of theatrical bias. Cibber's rehearsal behaviour is cited as an instance of theatrical partiality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theatrical merit includes action, show, and dress as legitimate aids
rubrics_metrics.description: The Advantages of Action, Show, and Dress on these Occasions are allowable, because the Merit consists in being capable of imposing upon us to our Advantage and Entertainment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stagecraft (gesture, look, voice, costume) legitimately contributes to the success of a play; theatrical embellishment can be justified when it heightens entertainment and moves the audience. Actors' artful management of expression and gesture is recognised as key to affecting passions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authors should distinguish what is theirs versus what is foreign
rubrics_metrics.description: My Reading makes such a strong impression upon me, that I should think my self a Cheat in my Way, if I should translate any thing from another Tongue, and not acknowledge it to my Readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When adapting or translating works (e.g., Colley Cibber adapting Corneille's Cid), authors should inform readers which elements are original and which are borrowed, both out of honesty and to allow proper critical judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetical justice: represent realistic human imperfection
rubrics_metrics.description: I cannot think it right to introduce a perfect or a faultless Man upon the Stage; not only because such a Character is improper to move Compassion, but because there is no such a thing in Nature. The most perfect Man has Vices enough to draw down Punishments upon his Head.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guideline for dramatists and poets: do not present absolutely virtuous characters as immune from misfortune. Tragedies where even good men meet unhappy ends can be morally and aesthetically richer — they move pity, teach humility, and better reflect nature. Aristotle and classical examples are invoked to support this.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy can justifiably represent virtuous sufferers
rubrics_metrics.description: The Instruction and Moral are much finer, where a Man who is virtuous in the main of his Character falls into Distress, and sinks under the Blows of Fortune at the End of a Tragedy, than when he is represented as Happy and Triumphant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a critical preference: tragic endings where virtuous characters suffer are more effective in teaching, softening the spectator, and correcting human pride than strictly 'poetical justice' where virtue is always rewarded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fair selection procedure for clubs to avoid partiality/corruption
rubrics_metrics.description: Issue writs to all and every of the Clubs ... requiring them to chuse out of their respective Bodies a Person of the greatest Merit, and to return his name to me before Lady-day ... so the Club over which I shall preside will be the very Flower and Quintescence of all other Clubs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrative guideline for forming an elective body: gather nominations from many independent clubs to reduce single-person bias, bribery, or charges of corruption; selection by peers aims to produce a representative and meritorious assembly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Praise should be proportionate to merit and is a fitting reward
rubrics_metrics.description: When Men of worthy and excelling Genius's have obliged the World with beautiful and instructive Writings, it is in the nature of Gratitude that Praise should be returned them, as one proper consequent Reward of their Performances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultural norm: public praise and the spread of 'fame' should reflect actual merit; praise encourages further beneficial labours and preserves authors' reputations beyond death. This functions as both moral endorsement and social incentive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism toward boastful medical advertisements and testimonials
rubrics_metrics.description: Sir William Read ... was one of the most pertinacious advertisers ... advertising that he had been 35 years in the practice of 'couching cataracts' ... Dr. Grant was another advertising oculist, illiterate and celebrated ... Mr. Moore sold a powder ... brought off worms of incredible length.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Spectator's inclusion of fictional patient-advertisements and satirical endorsements warns readers to be wary of extravagant cures and paid testimonials; readers should judge such claims critically rather than accept them at face value.
